opening.headline: The structure of the connector and remote MCP server solves the problem of not knowing how to connect an external app to the assistant.
body: You've probably thought about having your Assistant find Drive documents, read Slack messages, and create tickets for you. Some apps are connected directly from the list, while others are not in the list. Terms such as MCP, connector, and plug-in are mixed together, so the structure is not drawn, and the in-house system is not open to the outside, making it even more confusing.

In this lesson, we start from the point that a connector is a connection that exposes the functionality of an app to a tool in the assistant. Learn what the remote MCP server is, a common standard used by connectors, and how the connector directories of the three companies differ from custom connectors. Finally, we solve the structure of connecting the in-house inventory inquiry system to the remote MCP.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the relationship between a connector and a remote MCP server
You can distinguish between default connectors and custom connectors.

screens.title: I don't know how to connect an external app to the assistant.
screens.lead: First, let's look at the difficulties encountered when trying to connect an app. Think about where you don't see structure.

visual.alt: Assistant on the left, several in-house apps on the right, and a line with a question mark in between.
labels: Apps in and out of the list

paragraphs: I'd like the Assistant to find Drive documents, read Slack messages, and create tickets. However, some apps are connected directly from the list, and some apps are not in the list.
Terms such as MCP, connectors, and plugins are mixed together and do not depict the entire structure. The in-house system is even more confusing because it is not open to the outside world.
The question for this class is this. How are the apps and assistants connected?

screens.outro: First, let's think about the app you use.

screens.title: Which of the apps you are currently using can be connected?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think first before clicking.

items.prompt: What are the three apps you open most per day?
items.answer: Messenger, document storage, and task management tools are common answers. These apps are often where having the Assistant read to you is the most helpful. It's easier to decide where to connect if you write down the app name first.

items.prompt: What would you rather have the assistant read to you in that app, and what would you rather have it do for you?
items.answer: Things that are good for you to read are things like searching files, summarizing messages, and checking schedules, and things that are good for you to do for them are things like creating issues, sending messages, and registering schedules. The front corresponds to reading, and the back corresponds to writing.

items.prompt: Are reading and writing the same risk?
items.answer: It's different. Reading only exposes information if something goes wrong, but writing results in sending a message or changing data. So, when dealing with connectors, it is basic to separate read and write permissions.

screens.outro: Now that we have the eye to distinguish between reading and writing, let's start by looking at what a connector is.

screens.title: Connector: Export your app’s functionality as a tool in your assistant
screens.lead: Press the Next Step button to follow the app's functions as they are turned into tools one by one and added to the Assistant's toolbox.

visual.alt: The structure consists of an assistant on the left, a connector in the middle, and a list of app functions on the right.

steps.title: What is a connector?
steps.body: Connectors are connections that allow your assistant to get data from your apps and services and work within those services. Claude's instructions give examples of creating an issue in Linear, sending a message in Slack, and finding a file in Google Drive.

steps.title: App functions become tools
steps.body: The app has features like file search, sending messages, and creating issues. Connectors expose these functions as tools that your assistant can call. Rather than looking at app screens, the assistant calls tools and receives results.

steps.title: three types of tools
steps.body: Tools can be broadly defined in three ways. Tools that read data from connected apps, create, edit, and clear data, and act on behalf of users. Separating reading and writing tools makes it easier to determine which permissions to open.

steps.title: Apps from ChatGPT
steps.body: With ChatGPT, the app connects ChatGPT with services like Google Drive or Slack. Within a conversation, you can find files, summarize documents, browse messages, and even perform tasks supported by the app.

steps.title: Permissions remain the same
steps.body: User permissions for connected services remain the same. According to Claude's instructions, files or channels that cannot be viewed by humans cannot be accessed using connectors. A connector is a connection that bridges existing permissions to your assistant, rather than creating new permissions.

screens.outro: We need a standard to release the tool, so let's look at the remote MCP server next.

screens.title: Remote MCP server: Common specifications used by connectors
screens.lead: Compare how the connection path and required conditions change when switching between a local server and a remote server using a switch.

visual.alt: The assistant and MCP server are connected to the Internet, and the server wraps the app.
labels: Connection takes place in the cloud

states.label: local server
states.body: MCP is an open standard for AI applications to connect to tools and data. In the past, MCP servers only ran locally on users' computers. This method required the server and assistant to be on the same device, so they had to be installed and set up on one person's computer. If you want multiple people to use the company's system together, the same tasks must be repeated on each computer. Claude's instructions explain that there is a separate local way to configure Claude Desktop's settings file, which uses the user's network.

states.label: remote server
states.body: Nowadays, developers create servers and host them on the Internet, and there are remote MCP servers that AI apps communicate with over the Internet. A remote MCP server allows models to use tools and data located on the Internet. According to Claude's instructions, when you add a custom connector, the connection is made to the server in the Anthropic cloud rather than to the user's device. So the server must be reachable by Anthropic IP ranges from the public internet. Servers behind a private network or VPN must allow Anthropic IP ranges in their firewall to connect.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the structure of the specification, let's take a look at the three companies' directories and the custom connector creation screen.

screens.title: Connector directories for three companies and a custom connector creation screen
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the steps for finding and connecting connectors for each product. Notice how the paths for the default and custom connectors diverge.

visual.alt: Two screens showing Claude's connector directory and a custom connector creation screen.
labels: Authentication: Sign in now / Sign in when needed / No sign in
If it's not on the list, create your own

tabs.label: Claude Directory
tabs.body: In Claude, you can open Connectors from the + menu in a conversation, or you can view the connector directory in Connectors in Customize. Each connector in the directory has a page describing its purpose, read/write capabilities, and availability. Select the desired connector, click Connect or Install, follow the authentication instructions to allow access, and the connection will be established.

tabs.label: Customize Claude
tabs.body: For services that are not in the directory, click + Add in Connectors under Customize and select Add custom connector to connect. Enter your name and remote MCP server URL, press Continue, and you will see the authentication settings detected by Claude. Select the authentication method among Sign in now, Sign in when needed, or No sign in. If the server authenticates with an API key or static credentials instead of OAuth, you can put that in Request headers. After completing the settings, click Add and you are done.

tabs.label: ChatGPT
tabs.body: ChatGPT selects an app or a plugin containing the app in Plugins in Settings, and if necessary, click Install plugin to install and connect. After connecting, specify the app with @ in the conversation or select it from the + menu. Some apps require individual logins or use administrator-managed connections.

tabs.label: Basic and custom
tabs.body: The default connector is listed in the directory, so all you have to do is read the description and authenticate. A custom connector is a way to connect services that are not in your directory directly to a server URL. Customization has a high degree of freedom, but the person connecting must consider for themselves whether the server is trustworthy and whether the requested permissions are appropriate.

screens.outro: Now that we have compared the two types, let us point out the differences between the two and security precautions.

screens.title: Distinction between default connectors and custom connectors and security precautions
screens.lead: Please select one by one the passages highlighted in the explanation below. The difference between the two types and security precautions are explained.

data.text:
[Basic Connector]  
It is listed in the directory. Its purpose and read/write functions are described on the connector page; simply click Connect to authenticate.

[User-Defined Connector]  
Create it by manually entering the name and remote MCP server URL. You can also connect to services that have not been verified by Anthropic. After connecting, you can access the service and perform operations.

[Usage Restrictions and Roles]  
Free users are limited to one custom connector. In Team, when the owner adds a connector, each member connects.

[Security Note]  
Carefully review tool approval requests, and Use Allow always only on trusted servers and tools.; disable any unnecessary tools.

marks.span: It is listed in the directory.
marks.note: These are the characteristics of the basic connector. Each connector in the directory has a page explaining its purpose and read/write capabilities, so you can read about what it can do before connecting.

marks.span: Create it by manually entering the name and remote MCP server URL.
marks.note: The connection path for the custom connector. Because the server address is entered directly without going through a directory, the person connecting must check for themselves who runs the server.

marks.span: You can also connect to services that have not been verified by Anthropic.
marks.note: This is the freedom and risk of custom connectors. Once connected, Claude can access and work with those services, so we only connect to servers operated by trusted organizations.

marks.span: Free users are limited to one custom connector.
marks.note: This is a plan-specific limitation. Free users can only have one custom connector. If you need the number of connections, you should check the plan first.

marks.span: In Team, when the owner adds a connector, each member connects.
marks.note: It is a division of roles. Even if the owner adds a connector to the organization, members do not automatically access it, and each member must authenticate to use it. So each user's permissions remain the same.

marks.span: Use Allow always only on trusted servers and tools.
marks.note: Instructions for requesting tool approval. Clicking Always Allow for all requests eliminates human confirmation. It is safe to only use servers and tools that are safe to run without supervision, and turn off tools that are not needed.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the differences and points to note, let us unravel the structure of connecting in-house systems.

screens.title: Explanation: Structure for connecting in-house systems to remote MCP
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow the process of adding components, connection lines, and certification signs to the structure diagram step by step.

visual.alt: A structure that connects the assistant to the Internet, MCP server, and in-house system.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: I want my assistant to read my in-house inventory tracking system. This system is not publicly available, and there are no default connectors listed in the directory. So I take the route of connecting with a custom connector.

steps.title: Step 1: Create a remote MCP server
steps.body: Create a remote MCP server that provides inventory tracking tools. This server is the middle leg that receives the assistant's request, retrieves the value from the company's inventory system, and returns it. Name the tool to indicate what it does, such as inventory tracking.

steps.title: Step 2: Make the server reach
steps.body: Claude's connection is made to the Anthropic cloud, not your device, so its servers must be accessible from the public internet. If your server is behind a private network or VPN, your firewall must allow inbound connections from Anthropic IP ranges. The fact that you can reach it from your own computer is not grounds.

steps.title: Step 3: Register your custom connector
steps.body: In Customize, under Connectors, add a custom connector and enter its name and server URL. Select login as the authentication method. If it is a Team or Enterprise, the owner adds it to the organization, and each member connects to maintain each user's permissions.

steps.title: Step 4: Open only the reading tool and connect
steps.body: Since the purpose of the inventory is to read, we only open the reading tools and limit the writing tools that change the inventory. Turn off tools you don't need and look at approval requests carefully. If you start with a focus on reading, even if an incorrect action occurs, the result is limited to seeing the inventory value.

steps.title: Check results
steps.body: After connecting, ask an inventory question to check if the system values are correct. In the instructions, write that inventory questions are answered by querying the connected system. The structure is one line: Assistant, Internet, MCP server, and in-house system.

screens.outro: Now that we have solved the connection structure, let us summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Summarizes the contents of this class. As you read, try to answer the initial question: How are the apps and assistants connected?

paragraphs: The first question was how the app and assistant are connected. A connector is a connection that exposes the app's functions as a tool that the assistant can call, and a remote MCP server is a common standard that provides that tool over the Internet. The assistant works by calling tools rather than app screens.

The default connector reads the description from the directory, authenticates with Connect, and connects. Custom connectors connect by entering the name and server URL directly, and connect only to trusted servers because they can also reach unverified services. In Claude, the connection takes place in the Anthropic cloud, so the servers must be reachable.

The tool opens only the permissions you need, split between read and write. User permissions for connected services remain the same, approval requests are carefully checked, and tools you don't need are turned off.

Apps that are not listed in the first scene are now visible. If you have a server, you can connect to it with a custom connector. If you don't have a server, the next step is to first create a remote MCP server that exposes the tools. This flow is the same regardless of the product, so once you learn it, you can apply it to other assistants as well.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Opening a connection is easy, but once you do, it increases what Assistant can do in that app. Open for reading first, and only open for writing as much as absolutely necessary.

glossary.def: A connection that lets your assistant get data from and work with your apps and services.
An MCP server hosted on the Internet that provides tools and data to AI apps.
This screen contains a list and description of the default connectors that can be connected.
This is a connector created by directly entering the name and remote MCP server URL. Used when connecting to a service that is not in the directory.

misconceptions.myth: When you connect the connector, all data in the app will be opened.
misconceptions.fact: Connected services only open to the extent the user has permissions to do so. You cannot access files or channels that are not originally viewable.

misconceptions.myth: The remote MCP server is connected from my computer.
misconceptions.fact: According to Claude's instructions, the connection takes place in the Anthropic cloud. Even if the server you reach from your computer is in a private network, you need to set up a firewall.

misconceptions.myth: Apps that are not in the directory cannot be connected.
misconceptions.fact: If you have a remote MCP server, you can connect to it with a custom connector.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: A connector is a connection that exposes your app's functionality to a tool.
Remote MCP Server is a common standard for providing tools over the Internet.
Default connectors connect from the directory, custom connectors connect to a server URL.
Separate read and write and open only the permissions you need.

checks.q: I created the in-house inventory system as a remote MCP server, but the server is in a private network. How do I connect in Claude?
options: Connects directly from the user's device, so no additional setup is required
Since the connection is from the Anthropic cloud, you can reach it from the public internet or allow Anthropic IP ranges in your firewall.
Just change the server to run locally and you can connect to the cloud as well.
If you leave the server URL empty, it will be automatically found without authentication.
checks.explain: The remote MCP connection is made to a server in the Anthropic cloud, not to the user device, so the server must be reachable.

wrong.0: Since the connection is not made from the user's device, the server within the private network cannot be reached.
wrong.2: The local method is different from a cloud connection because it runs only on the user's computer.
wrong.3: For custom connectors, you must enter the name and server URL directly.

Connect with only the reading tools open and the writing tools limited.
